newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy ENI float set Monday, ENEL doubts state role.
newsitem.headline: Italy ENI float set Monday, ENEL doubts state role.

text.p: The second phase privatization of Italian state energy giant ENI gets underway Monday but the head of electricity utility Enel has questioned the state's role in future public selloffs.
The Treasury is due to announce Monday the amount of ENI shares it is floating after a first stage public sale last November.
The first tranche sale of 15 percent of the group at an offer price of 5,250 lire per share brought 6.3 trillion lire (US$4.0 billion) into state coffers.
The Italian press has suggested the state could sell between 15 and 25 percent, raising between 8.8 and 14.7 trillion lire.
Treasury, which will retain control of ENI, has not indicated its plans for further sell-offs of the energy group, which is Italy's largest publicly traded company.
ENI shares closed Friday up 3.02 percent at 7,302 lire after setting a year's high of 7,925 lire.
A series of worldwide road shows start Monday and the Italian public sale runs Oct 21 to 25. The share price will be fixed Oct 26 and trading is expected to start Oct 29.

A first tranche sale of Enel, the world's second-largest electricity group after EDF of France, is due to take place some time in 1997 after the privatization of state telecoms group Stet, slated for next Spring.
The selloff of Enel should have begun late last year but it was put off by a government crisis and lack of a sector regulating authority. The watchdog has now been created.
Enel Managing Director Franco Tato told a weekend conference on the liberalization of public services that privatization meant the state selling 51 percent of a company's shares.
"As long as the state holds on to a golden share there can't be a real separation. Either you privatise the whole of a company or you don't call it a privatization," he said.

"Surely private structures, at least in Italy, have shown that they are more efficient and more free than state structures," added Tato, who joined Enel in June from being MD at publishing group Mondadori, controlled by Silvio Berlusconi's Fininvest Spa.

The Anglo-Saxon concept of the golden share allows the state to continue to exercise particular powers in a privatised public company, including the right to name the chairman and being able to veto mergers or the entry of new shareholders.
The concept was adopted into Italian law in 1994 and was used for the first time with the ENI sale last November.
For Enel, it remains unclear whether the state intends to hold a golden share.

Giuliano Amato, head of Italy's Antitrust authority, told the weekend conference that it depended on the interests being served. "If one is more interested in maximising the gains from a company you don't use a golden share, but if the main idea is to keep a hand in the company, then you do," he said.

European Union Consumer Affairs Commissioner Emma Bonino said she agreed with Tato. "European public services can and must be run on a market basis with independent regulators and without direct management on the part of the state through a golden share or exclusive rights," she told the forum.

A cautious Industry Minister Pierluigi Bersani told the conference the government had still time to study the question. But if a golden share existed "it will have to be used in a moderate and basic way. The reason for its existence must be motivated by the clear needs of collective national interests."
Industry under-secretary Umberto Carpi was quoted as saying in Sunday's left-wing L'Unita newspaper he believed Tato was just being provocative.

"Enel is not just an industry like any other, you can't talk of producing energy being like making cakes...Enel operates in a strategic sector for the country and similar worries have also been expressed in other European countries," he said.
